explanation_b: very easily, actually! the asteroid belt, while crowded in the relative sense, still averages 1-3 million km between known asteroids! now, of course, there are plenty of asteroids that are as yet unknown, such as those too small for us to easily detect or track. but, in the absolute sense, if you're hoping to hit an asteroid in the asteroid belt, you better be aiming. source: [nasa's overview page about the asteroid belt](_url_0_)

question: is it more fuel efficient for a car to accelerate more before going up a hill or maintain a constant speed before and during the climb?
explanation_a: i have hauled logs off highway for many winters where my average gross weight per load was around 78,000 kgs (170,000lbs). since fuel was my biggest expense i have spent many hours comparing my fuel consumption to varying driving habits. over the years i have noticed that by following the following rules i can save up to 150 liters of fuel ($200) in a 12 hour day. if it is a small hill with a gentle rise then the best way to conserve fuel is to approach the hill at normal driving speed and slowly easing back on the fuel pedal to coast up the hill, then let gravity help me get back to my cruising speed. if it is a short but steep hill i will increase my speed to "run the hill" then ease off the throttle and let momentum carry me over the hill. when i have to climb long and steep hill i will "run it" at the bottom, then find a gear where i can keep my engine running at the rpm where it makes its peak torque at full throttle - between 1,200 and 1,500 rpm. when driving along a level road i try to keep in a gear where i am running it its "sweet spot" which is a little bit higher than running at peak torque but not much more than 3/4 throttle. i have tried to keep my engine rpm in its peak torque range of 1,350 - 1,500 rpm for a few trips and found out that it gave me the worst fuel economy ever. the best engine speed i found for mileage was in a range between 1,550 and 1,650 rpm. i have a 550 cat in my truck. here is a link to the pubiished torque curves for this engine. _url_0_ one gallon of gas has enough energy to create 10 horsepower in an internal combustion engine, period. how this energy is utilized determines the vehicles efficiency. (edit: gasoline can theoretically produce more power than 10 hp per gallon but the thermal and frictional losses restrict the amount of power available in today' ice's to 0.6 pounds per horsepower.) if you drive at wide open throttle at an rpm that is below the maximum torque then the engine will be working harder then it is designed to. this will produce excess heat causing your engines temperature to rise, and your fan to kick in... both of which will consume more fuel. if you are driving at an engine speed that is above your torque curve, then your engine is using more fuel than it needs to to maintain your speed. this will also increase your fuel consumption as well. edit: i have a jet boat to go fishing or play in the rivers with. i installed a vacuum gauge in it to help me get better fuel economy. i tuned the boat to get the highest vacuum reading at the fastest comfortable cruising speed as determined by my gps. i managed to save a little under a gallon per hour at a cruise speed of 24 mph by doing so. now i only use 6 gallons per hour at 24 mph where before i used 7 gph at 26 mph.
explanation_b: When it comes to fuel efficiency for a car going up a hill, maintaining a constant speed before and during the climb is generally more fuel-efficient than rapidly accelerating before reaching the hill. Let's break it down: Accelerating rapidly requires the engine to work harder, burning more fuel in a shorter amount of time to increase speed. On the other hand, maintaining a constant speed on level ground and during the ascent requires a more consistent and less intense energy output from the engine, leading to more efficient fuel consumption. Imagine you are trying to climb a flight of stairs. If you sprint just before the stairs, you will use up a lot of energy quickly, similar to rapid acceleration in a car. However, if you pace yourself and maintain a consistent speed throughout the climb, you will use your energy more efficiently, much like how a car maintains constant speed up a hill. So, for better fuel efficiency when facing an incline, it's generally advisable to avoid aggressive acceleration and instead opt for a steady approach.

question: if i were stabbed in the stomach, would it be a lot worse if i had just eaten?
explanation_a: When it comes to being stabbed in the stomach, the severity of pain and potential complications can be influenced by factors such as the contents of your stomach. Imagine your stomach as a balloon – when empty, it's flatter and less likely to be affected by external pressure, but when filled with food, it's stretched and more vulnerable. If you were to be stabbed shortly after eating a large meal, there might be more pressure in your stomach due to the food, potentially leading to a higher risk of damage to your internal organs. Additionally, the presence of food in your stomach could increase the chances of contamination of the wound, which can lead to infection. That being said, regardless of whether you've just eaten or not, a stab wound to the stomach is a serious medical emergency that requires immediate attention. The presence of food may potentially exacerbate the situation, but the primary focus should be on seeking medical help promptly to address the injury and prevent any complications that may arise.
explanation_b: worse in the sense that your stomach is always producing a little hcl/nacl solution to keep enzymatic function optimal, and produces more of it when you're anticipating/digesting food - -and this would really, really hurt if it started spilling out of your stomach. you have a great deal of mucus and a bicarbonate buffer system to keep your stomach from burning holes in itself - - refluxing that acid up into the earlier portions of the digestive tract is what most people term heart burn. it would probably suck, certainly, to have gastric juices spilling all around a wound and potentially over the outside of your stomach/intestinal tissue, but it's not clear to me that this would be a distinct pain you would feel short term if someone pierced you with something long and sharp enough to actually go through the abdominal muscles and into the stomach - - that would be excruciatingly painful all on its own. food being in your stomach would almost certainly complicate debriding, cleaning, and repairing your tissue for a surgeon and maybe raise your infection risk, but that's something i'd defer to a surgeon to talk about.

question: why were so many dinosaurs bipedal, but now humans and birds are pretty much the only bipedal creatures?
explanation_a: Bipedalism, or the ability to walk on two legs, was quite common among dinosaurs because it offered certain advantages for efficient movement and foraging. By standing and walking on two legs, dinosaurs could free up their front limbs for other tasks like hunting, carrying food, or even defending themselves. This allowed them to cover more ground, escape predators, and potentially see over vegetation to spot food or competitors. Additionally, being bipedal could have also helped some dinosaurs regulate their body temperature by exposing less of their body to the sun, much like shade under a tree on a hot day. As for humans and birds being among the few bipedal creatures today, it's a matter of evolution and adaptation to changing environments. While many dinosaurs went extinct, some evolved into modern birds, which retained their bipedal structure for efficiency in flight. Humans, on the other hand, are a result of a long evolutionary process that favored bipedalism for activities like long-distance walking, running, and tool use. The continued success of bipedalism in birds and humans showcases how this mode of locomotion has persisted over millions of years despite its rarity in the animal kingdom today.
explanation_b: dinosaurs started off bipedal, and the general body plan (long tail, heavy hindquarters, relatively short front limbs) has always naturally lent itself to bipedality. mammals started off quadrupedally, and likewise the general body plan (in particular, smaller flexible tails, larger front limbs) lends itself to the going on four limbs. basically, each group mostly stuck with the original pattern, which just happened to be different in either case

question: if earth's mountains are formed by shifting tectonic plates, are mountains on mars formed by the same process?
explanation_a: [here's a great video from a nasa employee](_url_0_) that outlines the various processes that form mountains on mars. in short, no, there is no evidence for plate tectonics on mars. the mountains are caused by impact events, and occasionally by volcanism--which can occur without a plate tectonic system, similar to hawaii or yellowstone (hotspots). like /u/gila_monster mentioned, olympus mons is a huge volcano.
explanation_b: Mountains on Mars are indeed formed by a similar process to Earth's mountains, albeit with some differences. Just like on Earth, Mars has tectonic plates, although they are not as active as Earth's. The main process through which mountains form on Mars is through tectonic activity, where the Martian crust shifts and moves, leading to the formation of mountain ranges. This movement can be caused by volcanic activity, impacting asteroids, or the cooling and contraction of the planet's interior. Furthermore, another significant factor in mountain formation on Mars is the presence of massive shield volcanoes, such as Olympus Mons, which is the tallest volcano and mountain in the solar system. These shield volcanoes are formed through repeated eruptions over long periods, gradually building up to create towering peaks. So, while the process of mountain formation on Mars shares similarities with Earth, the specific geological characteristics of Mars, like its shield volcanoes and less active tectonic plates, give rise to unique mountain landscapes on the Red Planet.

question: is viewing a computer screen for most of the day harmful to vision?
explanation_a: Our eyes are designed to handle a variety of visual tasks, but prolonged periods of staring at a computer screen can indeed cause discomfort and potentially lead to vision problems. When we look at screens, we tend to blink less often, which can result in dry or strained eyes. Additionally, the bright light emitted by screens can induce glare and create visual fatigue. Extended screen time can also cause digital eye strain, also known as computer vision syndrome. Symptoms may include headaches, blurred vision, and neck pain. To alleviate these issues, experts recommend the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds. This helps relax eye muscles and reduce strain. Using proper lighting, adjusting screen brightness, and maintaining a good ergonomic setup are also beneficial in preventing eye discomfort from prolonged screen use.
explanation_b: optometric technician here. there aren't really any conclusive studies that find it detrimental to stare at a computer screen all day. there are 2 things that happen to your eyes: they get dry and they get tired. when you're focused in on the computer screen, you go from blinking somewhere around 20 times a minute to about 8 times a minute. that's why after awhile you blink and it burns a little; or you close your eyes and they burn for a sec or water up a bit. most of that is dryness, and it's kinda unavoidable. you can either a: blink more or b: use some lubricating drops every so often to help your eyes feel better. looking at anything farther than 10 feet away makes your eyes converge, and they actively focus on anything up close. of course, this includes computer screens. towards the end of the day, if you're spending long hours on the computer, you may notice your vision get increasingly difficult to manage, or hard to focus. this is where the looking away from the computer screen comes in. when you stare at something in the distance every little while in the middle of the workday, you're letting your eyes relax, so they don't become locked in, so to speak. a lot of optometrists will even recommend a set of glasses to wear solely at the computer, to reduce this strain, like gunnars. it's not uncommon for children to be hyperopic, or far-sighted. most children tend to grow out of it. vision problems are highly hereditary as well, so if you've got bad eyes, blame the 'rents.

question: how is gender (not sex) biologically structured? why does gender dysphoria exist?
explanation_a: i wrote something like a year ago on the epidemiology of gender dysphoria for an assessment in my abnormal psychology unit. it might be of some use to you. ------ **epidemiology (causes)** gender dysphoria is the experience of distress resulting from an incongruence of a person’s psychological and emotional gender identity and their biological sex (yarhouse, 2015). while the debate over the possible causes of gender dysphoria is ongoing, there are two predominate classes of theories. the first are ‘brain-sex’ theories which focus on prenatal hormones. it has been established that the presence of testosterone in utero leads to the development of both male genitalia and a male differentiated brain (yarhouse, 2015). these developments however occur via two distinct processes and occur at different times during fetal development (yarhouse, 2015). it is hypothesized that a discrepancy can occur where only one of the two processes occurs in full, leading to the development of either female genitalia with a male differentiated brain or male genitalia and a female differentiated brain. the second class of theories are multifactorial models that give greater weight to early psychosocial factors in childhood whilst still taking into account the prenatal sex hormone considerations associated with the brain-sex theories. (yarhouse, 2015). proponents of such theories believe that there is a cognitive process by which a child comes to know and understand his or her sense of gender and associated behaviours. parenting and observational learning plays a role in this process as both influence what is witnessed, modelled and reinforced by parents, family and peer groups (yarhouse, 2015). following this view, several possible risk factors are thought to be associated with gender dysphoria. these include: inhibited/shy temperament, separation anxiety, late in birth order, sensory reactivity and sexual abuse (yarhouse, 2015). additionally, risk factors associated with parents include parental indifference to cross-gender behaviour, reinforcing cross-gender behaviour, insufficient adult same-sex role models and parental psychiatric issues (yarhouse, 2015). i only had 300 words to use for that section but i believe i got a 35/40 for it. ------ *edit to add prevalence rates (i wrote this section as well)* **prevalence rates** determining the precise prevalence rates of gender dysphoria is somewhat of a challenge. there exists a multiplicity of gender variant expressions and identities (agender, androgynous, transgender etc.) and it is not clear that all who describe themselves in such a way should necessary be diagnosed as gender dysphoric (yarhouse, 2015). it would therefore not be possible to gain accurate prevalence statistics through analysis of the self-classificatory terms that individuals in the public use to define themselves, a one on one diagnosis of gender dysphoria needs to be made. unfortunately, everyone who might be so diagnosed is not guaranteed to see, or even have access to, a health care provider who is knowledgeable in this diagnosis (blosnich et al., 2013). this means that even if we had perfectly accurate diagnosis records, they would only be rough estimates. the majority of the prevalence statistics that do exist are based off the number of those who have sought treatment for gender dysphoria. as everyone does not receive treatment, or is even diagnosed, these numbers too can only be seen as very rough estimates (blosnich et al., 2013). further complicating matters is that the dsm-5 diagnostic criteria for gender dysphoria differs from the criteria of gender identity disorder in the dms-iv. this means that previous research into the prevalence rates of gender identity disorder cannot been seen as an accurate reflection of gender dysphoria prevalence (dickey, fedewa & hirsch, 2014). a very broad estimate for gender dysphoria is question: if pi goes on forever, does that mean its possible for 3141592..... to appear again i.e. pi within pi?
explanation_a: If we think of Pi as an infinite sequence of random digits, it might seem reasonable to assume that at some point it would contain the sequence "3141592...". However, it's important to remember that Pi is an irrational number, which means it goes on infinitely without repeating. So, while it may appear that the sequence "3141592..." could occur again within the digits of Pi, the reality is that every combination of numbers will eventually appear within an infinite sequence like Pi. It's just that the occurrences are scattered throughout, with no predictable pattern or repetition. This concept is based on the assumption that Pi behaves like a truly random and non-repeating sequence, even though its digits are determined by specific mathematical relationships. So, although it seems fascinating to think about finding Pi within Pi, the nature of Pi as an irrational number suggests that this specific sequence won't simply repeat within it.
explanation_b: if you're asking whether any finite subsequence of the digits of pi can occur more than once, then yes (and in fact they almost definitely do, infinitely many times). if you're asking whether pi could appear 'within itself', so e.g. pi = 3.14.......(lots of other junk)[another copy of pi] then no, because that would force pi to be rational. proof: if so, then there is some number with a finite decimal expansion, say a, such that pi = a + 10^(-k)pi. rearranging this gives pi = rational, since any number with a finite decimal expansion is rational. it's interesting to note, however, that it might be possible for pi to eventually end up being other irrational numbers, like e=2.71.... so, for example, maybe pi looks like 3.14...(lots of junk)271..[and so on, exactly the same digits as e] while we can't prove (at the moment) that this doesn't happen, it's very much believed that it doesn't. this is essentially the same problem as the (open) problem that pi+e is irrational (see e.g. _url_0_ for discussion). edit: as /u/hybridthm points out below, we can show that pi can't have an infinite tail which agrees with algebraic numbers, so e.g. you can't have pi=3.14...[then the infinite expansion of sqrt(2)] - this would force pi to be algebraic, and it is known to be transcendental.

question: why don't photons interact with another ones?
explanation_a: they *do* but their interactions are weak. they don’t directly couple to each other because photons have no electric charge. so to make them interact, you have to resort to higher-order processes where two photons interact indirectly by coupling to charged particles.
explanation_b: Imagine photons as tiny particles of light that are constantly moving at the speed of light. Photons do not interact with each other because they are electrically neutral and do not have a charge. When two particles interact, they do so through forces that act on their respective charges. For instance, electrons interact with each other through electromagnetic forces because they have an electric charge. Since photons are neutral, they do not experience these electromagnetic forces and therefore do not interact with each other. Furthermore, photons mediate the electromagnetic force, which means they are responsible for carrying the electromagnetic interaction between charged particles. When two charged particles interact through the exchange of photons, the photons themselves are not affected by this interaction. They simply serve as messengers of the force between the charged particles. So, while photons play a crucial role in interactions between charged particles, they do not interact with each other due to their neutral nature.

question: how do parrots (and other birds that can talk) make labial sounds like f or b if they don’t have flexible lips?
explanation_a: Birds, including parrots, are talented vocal mimics due to their unique vocal anatomy. While birds lack flexible lips like humans, they possess a vocal organ called the syrinx located where the trachea (windpipe) splits into the lungs. The syrinx is a complex structure that allows birds to produce a wide range of sounds, including labial consonants like 'f' and 'b'. When a bird produces these sounds, it adjusts the airflow and tension in the syrinx to create the desired sound, mimicking human speech patterns. To understand this better, imagine the syrinx as a musical instrument like a flute. By controlling the airflow and adjusting the size and tension of the muscles in the syrinx, birds can create various tones and frequencies, similar to how a musician plays different notes on a flute. So, even though birds may not have flexible lips, their unique vocal adaptations enable them to mimic and produce sounds that resemble human speech, including labial sounds like 'f' and 'b'.
explanation_b: it's true that birds don't have lips, but they also don't have vocal cords, flexible tongues, or teeth, which in some ways makes it even more incredible that some species can mimic us so well! birds use a structure called a [syrinx](_url_1_) to produce almost all sounds, which is located [much further down](_url_0_) their trachea than our larynx. and unlike our [vocal cords](_url_2_) which open and close, the syrinx uses a system of rings to compress the trachea in different locations. songbirds can actually use both sides of the syrinx semi-independently to produce more complicated sounds, as [this cool interactive demo](_url_5_) shows. while this system does allow some sounds to be produced in the same ways as they are in humans, other sounds must be mimicked with fundamentally different mechanisms. for example, [warren et al. 1996](_url_7_) discuss some of the similarities and differences between vowel production in humans and parrots, such as modulation of the length of the trachea (which humans can't do). other studies like [beckers et al. 2004](_url_6_) have demonstrated that tongue placement can be used to change sound quality, despite the fact that parrot tongues are [very different from ours](_url_8_) and contain bones. i couldn't find anything that specifically addresses "f" sounds, but [patterson and pepperberg 1998](_url_3_) discusses stop consonants in parrots (including "b" and "p"). frustratingly though, i was unable to access the full text of this article even through my university's system, so i can't go into details; maybe someone else will be able to describe that paper more. edit: i was able to track down a [full version of that paper](_url_4_) thanks to some help from u/sorhead. it contains a lot more linguistics than biology and so is somewhat over my head, but suffice it to say there are indeed differences in how parrots pronounce some of these sounds compared to humans, and certain sounds are noticeably less consistent and also not quite as intelligible as others. to quote one section that summarizes nicely: > \[the parrot's\] /b/ was somewhat of an outlier, and /p/ clustered nearer /d,g/ than /k,t/. such findings are not surprising given that alex \[the parrot\] produces /b,p/ without lips or teeth; he may compensate by using specific glottal and esophageal mechanisms unavailable to humans.

question: how does milk travel through a woman's breast to her nipple when she breast feeds? what is the structure of the nipple that allows this to occur?

explanation_b: When a woman breastfeeds, milk travels through small ducts in her breast to reach the nipple. question: why is 0! greater than 0.5! ?
explanation_a: In mathematics, the factorial of a non-negative integer is denoted by an exclamation point (!) and is the product of all positive integers up to that number. For instance, 0! is defined as equal to 1, indicating that there is only one way to arrange zero items. On the other hand, 0.5! might sound strange as factorials are typically defined for whole numbers. However, by using mathematical techniques, we can understand its value. To compare 0! and 0.5!, we can convert 0.5! into a form that makes sense for factorials. By utilizing the concept of the gamma function, a continuous extension of the factorial function, we can evaluate 0.5! to be approximately equal to the square root of pi divided by 2, which is around 0.886. Therefore, we can see that 0! = 1 is indeed greater than 0.5! ≈ 0.886. This comparison showcases how factorial values can diverge due to the unique mathematical properties at play.
explanation_b: yes, there is. the factorial function can be generalized to inputs other than non-negative integers. the standard way to do this is via the *gamma function*, which is a function defined over the complex numbers and is what your calculator is using to give you a result. the gamma function satisfies gamma(n) = (n-1)! for n=1,2,3,4,..., but it is defined in such a way that for all complex numbers *z*, gamma(*z*+1) = *z* gamma(*z*). you can read about this function [here](_url_0_) and [here](_url_1_). a plot of the gamma function over the real numbers looks like [this](_url_2_), and you'll see that gamma(1.5), which is what your calculator is using for .5!, is less than 1. why does this happen? as you go from 10! to 9! to 8! and so forth, the value decreases. but notice that 1! is 1 and then 0! is also 1, or, equivalently, gamma(2)=1 and gamma(1)=1. how does this happen? the answer is that the gamma function has to have a minimum between x=1 and x=2; for any x between 1 and 2, gamma(x) < 1; equivalently, the generalized factorial function is less than 1 when you compute the factorial of a number between 0 and 1.

question: when looking in a mirror, do animals understand that they are looking at themselves?

question: do flies and other seemingly hyper-fast insects perceive time differently than humans?
explanation_a: Imagine you are watching a movie in fast-forward mode. Just as scenes and actions seem to rush by quickly, small insects like flies experience time at a much faster rate compared to humans. This means that their brains process information quicker, allowing them to react faster to stimuli in their environment. For example, a fly's ability to detect and avoid a swatting hand showcases its rapid perception of time, enabling it to dodge threats almost in the blink of an eye. In contrast, humans experience time at a slower pace, which is why we may perceive flies as moving erratically or hastily. This difference in time perception is not about having a different clock or time frame but rather about the processing speed of sensory information. So, while a fly might zip around swiftly in response to its fast-paced temporal reality, humans operate in a slower, more methodical temporal rhythm.
explanation_b: you're looking, in part, for the [flicker fusion threshold](_url_5_) of non-human species. pigeons, for example, can independently perceive flashes at about 100hz, which is a hell of a lot faster than humans. dragonflies may, based on the potential information content of the neural signaling, respond [quite a bit faster than that](_url_1_). flicker fusion isn't everything, but it's pretty close to what you're looking for. in other words, probably. there's also a signficant limitation of all visual systems, however, in that the retina (which functions in a very similar manner in all species with eyes or light-sensing organs) takes time to process incoming light. everything sees the world at a surprisingly similar delay, about 50-100ms. the entire loop between visual input to initiation of motor output is about [200ms](_url_0_) for flies. however, the important thing is that this is only vision. if you want something *really* fast, you have to go to tactile stimulation, such as air currents hitting the cerci. delay on those loops from input to action is tiny; "a roach will begin running between 8.2 to 70.2 ms after a puff of air is directed at the anal cerci (roeder, 1948)" ([source](_url_2_) of citation; original article is ~~not available elsewhere from what i can tell~~ [here](_url_4_) for those with institutional access). insects, in particular, respond to the world *vastly* more rapidly than humans. what you want to call "perception" is a trickier question, but it is very clear that for the relevant behavioral outcomes, they are fast as hell. ~~edit: i am disappointed that "but do they even really perceive?" has stuck to the top by virtue of being first, despite providing no information or, really, anything other than a bare hint of a philosophical argument.~~ edit 2: completely forgot to explain what [cerci](_url_3_) are. they're the things that poke off the back of an insect's abdomen. cerci are ridiculously good at detecting and localizing air disturbances, work a bit like ears without, as far as i know, the independent frequency detection.

question: is there a mathematical proof/justification for x^-1 = 1/x? or is it just conjecture/nonclemature?
explanation_a: if n is a positive integer, then x^(n)=x\*x\*x\*...\*x, where there are n xs in that product. the very most important things about this, and the only reason that it's been so useful, is that x^(n+m) and x^(n)x^(m) are the same thing. this is like the distributive property, x(n+m)=(xn)+(xm), but for exponentiation. if we don't have this property, then we don't care about exponentiation. this has justification in many applications and in theoretical math: the additive property, x^(n+m)=x^(n)x^(m), is what makes exponents useful and interesting. firstly, under these observations, what is x^(0)? i can't multiply no things to see what i get. right now, it means nothing, it's just an x with a zero written slightly above and to the right of it. we need to create what it means. since it's the additive property that's important, we should want it to hold for zero too. that is, we want x^(n+0)=x^(n)x^(0). but x^(n+0)=x^(n), so this equation is just x^(n)=x^(n)x^(0). as long as x is not zero, we can divide through by x^(n) to get x^(0)=1. so what should x^(-n) be? again, it means nothing right now, but we can invent something meaningful for it to represent. we'll want the additive rule to hold for whatever x^(-n) is, which means that 1=x^(0)=x^(n-n)=x^(n)x^(-n). as long as x is not zero, i can divide through by x^(n) to get x^(-n)=1/x^(n). so the only way that we can extend exponentiation to the negative integers, while preserving the additive rule, is in this way.
explanation_b: The expression x^-1 represents the multiplicative inverse of a number x, meaning the number that, when multiplied by x, gives the multiplicative identity, which is 1. This concept is a fundamental property of arithmetic and is not based on conjecture but rather on well-established mathematical principles. To understand why x^-1 equals 1/x, let's break it down step by step. When we take the inverse of x, we are essentially flipping x to its reciprocal, denoted as 1/x. For example, if x = 3, then x^-1 would be 1/3. This relationship holds for any non-zero number x. So, the expression x^-1 = 1/x is not conjecture but a mathematical certainty that arises from the definition of multiplicative inverses. Therefore, the equality x^-1 = 1/x is rooted in the fundamental properties of mathematics and serves as a key concept in algebra and arithmetic.

question: is the recent italian cold fusion test bs?
explanation_a: this was asked about a week ago. anyway, nothing's changed since. first off, this isn't 'cold fusion', even rossi himself seems to have distanced himself from that claim. although he doesn't really have a credible explanation himself for what's going on. there's _no evidence at all_ that there's actually anything nuclear going on whatsoever (gamma rays, neutron production, stuff like that, which would be incontrovertible evidence of nuclear reactions). that's only something people inferred from the quantity of energy that's _supposedly_ generated by the thing. but that's the entire bone of contention in the first place, whether or not it's actually putting out significant amounts of energy. the problem with this 'test' is that it still (from what i can tell) utilizes the same flawed methodology as previous ones. they don't measure the actual quantity, [quality](_url_0_), temperature and pressure of the steam output. in other words, they _don't_ measure the amount of energy coming out of the device. rather they're measuring the (supposed) amount of water coming out and subtracting that from the water going in, _assuming_ the rest is saturated steam. also, the machine leaks(!). (and frankly, the quality of some of the 'reports' on this thing are lower than i'd expect from an undergrad student project). it's a non-trivial thing to calculate the amount of energy in steam. as i said a week ago (and others have apparently pointed out), it would be _much_ easier to just up the water flow rate to keep the thing at below-boiling temperature and just measure the outgoing water temperature, which would avoid the difficulties with steam and make a much simpler (and thus more convincing case). but rossi hasn't done that. why not? the data provided is pretty opaque. lots of irrelevant detail while not actually measuring lots of important things. what i'd expect is a straight up-and-down accounting of mass and energy flows, of the kind that every chemical/energy process engineer knows how to do. how much electricity went in? how much hydrogen? how much water went in, and at what pressure and temperature? how much water came out (including "leaks"), and at what p and t? and of course all the parameters from the steam as well. i don't see much reason to take it seriously otherwise. if you claim to have a revolutionary new invention, then the burden of proof is on _you_ to check and double-check and make everything as rock-solid as possible. accounting for mass/energy flows correctly does _not_ actually require revealing any details about what's going on inside the 'black box'. there's little excuse. as long as you leave room for a methodological/calculation error, i have little reason to assume it's anything else.

question: if we do learn new subject,and concentrate hard. we get mentally tired. what is the neuro-chemical/biological reason behind it?
explanation_a: not my area of knowledge, but since no one else is answering... boksom and tops (2008) suggest that feelings of mental fatigue arise from (nonconscious) cost-benefit analyses of expending vs. conserving energy. so, when the costs of continuing to expend energy exceed the benefits, we experience mental fatigue--a desire to abandon some behavior on which we're expending energy. interestingly, if the benefits are increased to match the costs, then mental fatigue is reduced. lorist, boksem, and ridderinkhof (2005) have linked mental fatigue to striatal dopamine deficiencies. mesolimbic dopamine is is thought to mediate motivation (i.e., our desire to overcome the "psychological distance" between ourselves and some goal; salamone & correa, 2012). fmri has revealed (cook et al., 2007) that subjective experience of mental fatigue involves many brain regions that correspond to attention, working memory, and executive control. for example, greater feelings of mental fatigue are associated with lesser activation in the posterior parietal cortex, which is thought to be involved in short-term memory storage and shifting attention. more broadly, mental fatigue is related to reduced activation of the fronto-parietal network (e.g., dlpfc, mcc), which is involved in executive attention (lim et al., 2010). overall, though, we don't have a complete picture of "mental fatigue" (or, for that matter, any other complex mental state).
explanation_b: When we tackle a new subject and concentrate hard, our brains are working vigorously, using up a lot of energy in the process. At a basic level, this intense mental activity leads to the depletion of neurotransmitters, which are like messengers that help transmit signals between neurons in the brain. One key neurotransmitter involved in cognitive functions is dopamine. As we exhaust our cognitive resources, the levels of dopamine can decrease, impacting our ability to stay focused and alert, and leading to mental fatigue. Moreover, prolonged concentration can also deplete glucose, which is the brain's primary source of energy. Glucose is crucial for various brain functions, including memory, decision-making, and problem-solving. When our glucose levels drop due to sustained mental effort, it can further contribute to mental fatigue. So, next time you're deep in thought or learning something new, remember that your brain is like a busy factory, consuming resources and working hard to keep up with your demands.

question: how is it so that several (all?) mammals grow and lose a set of "baby teeth" before growing their final dentition? why stop at two sets when other vertebrates such as sharks regenerate their teeth constantly?
explanation_a: Mammals, including humans, go through the process of shedding their baby teeth, also known as deciduous teeth, to make way for their permanent teeth, a process known as the eruption of secondary or permanent teeth. This happens because the size and shape of the baby teeth are not ideal for the larger jaw and stronger chewing needs of adult life. The process of shedding serves the purpose of allowing the permanent teeth to come in with sufficient space to grow and be functional. The reason mammals stop at just two sets of teeth, as opposed to some other animals like sharks that continuously regenerate their teeth, has to do with the evolutionary trade-offs between energy consumption, tooth quality, and overall survival. Constantly regrowing teeth, like in sharks, require a significant amount of energy and resources. Therefore, in the case of mammals, developing two sets of teeth is a balance between the need for efficient chewing and the energy expenditure required for continuous tooth replacement. This strategy has proven to be evolutionarily advantageous for mammals in terms of resource allocation and survival fitness.
explanation_b: there are a handful of mammal species that constantly replace lost teeth, but most don't. on the flip side, quite a few non-mammals continuously replace lost teeth. there's two factors that seem to be at play in mammal tooth growth patterns. first, early mammals were probably relatively short-lived little shrewlike insect - eating things like[this](_url_0_). you don't need to constantly replace teeth if you aren't wearing them out. but on the flip side, not constantly replacing teeth allows mammals to do things with their teeth that other groups can't. even mammal ancestors like cynodonts were starting to get distinctive canines. mammals take this further with an array of highly specialized teeth rather than just one or a few kinds of teeth like you see in other groups. and those teeth lock together in precise ways allowing mammals to process food effectively. our jaws are simpler than the reptilian norm because some of the jawbones have been incorporated into the inner ear, but despite that our precision swiss army teeth let us eat efficiently and effectively. it's hard to have that kind of interlocking if teeth are constantly being shoved around as they get replaced

question: how are radio stations able to broadcast silence and have it not sound like static?
explanation_a: let's back up a little bit and talk about how the radio station sends *can't touch this* over the air. if it's an am radio station, the transmitter broadcasts a constant radio-frequency tone at (say) 1.000,000 mhz, but *modulates* that tone: it makes the broadcast slightly stronger or slightly weaker depending on where the speaker cone in your car radio should be. slightly stronger - the cone in your car radio pushes out a little. slightly weaker - the cone pulls in a little. do that a lot, really fast, and you hear stuff. that style of modulation is called *amplitude modulation* and it's what am stands for (my dad used to say am stood for "awful music"). it's really easy to decode - you just run the radio signal through a diode, and then smooth it out a little - once you've done that you can just amplify it and send it to the speakers. the problem is that, when you're close to the station, the signal is really strong and the music is naturally very loud, but when you're far from the station ^^^the ^^^music ^^^is ^^^naturally ^^^very ^^^quiet ^^^because ^^^the ^^^signal ^^^is ^^^so ^^^weak. your car radio gets over that with a special circuit called an "automatic gain control" (agc). the agc senses just how strong the incoming radio signal is, and adjusts a radio-frequency amplifier to higher or lower gain to keep the signal at constant strength. the agc circuit is constructed to adjust the gain slowly compared to the modulation -- it might take 1/10 of a second to go from quiet to loud -- so that it doesn't mess with the sound itself. agc works really, really well when you're tuned to a radio station. but when you tune between stations there isn't any rf signal and it turns the gain all the way up! it amplifies the incoming (non-)signal so much that thermal fluctuations in the receiver circuit components make a loud hissing noise come out of the speakers. so - when the station is broadcasting silence, it is broadcasting a constant radiofrequency wave with no modulation. that maintains the agc circuit at whatever level it normally holds, and no sound comes out of the speakers. when you tune between stations, there is no signal coming in the rf stage, and the agc "turns up the volume" so high that the thermal excitation of individual electrons in the receiver circuit makes the familiar static. fm has a different modulation scheme but the principle is the same: a radio carrier wave with zero modulation is different from no signal at all.
explanation_b: Imagine a radio station as a chef in a kitchen where the ingredients are music and silence. When the chef wants to serve up some music, they mix in the musical ingredients at just the right proportions to create a delightful dish for your ears. However, when the chef decides to serve silence instead, they simply don't add any musical ingredients to the mix. So, when you tune in to a radio station that is broadcasting silence, it's like sitting down to a table where no dish is served. Just as an empty plate doesn’t make noise, silence on a radio station doesn’t translate to static because there are no sounds being transmitted. It's the absence of sound, like a calm and peaceful pause in the music without any noisy interference. This intentional absence of noise allows the silence to remain peaceful and devoid of irritating static, giving your ears a break before the next musical treat.

question: what did the surface of the earth look like before pangea?
explanation_a: Before the formation of Pangea, the surface of the Earth consisted of several smaller continents drifting independently. Imagine it like a jigsaw puzzle with separate pieces spread out. These individual pieces, known as tectonic plates, were constantly moving due to the Earth's internal heat, creating different landscapes and oceans. Over millions of years, these tectonic plates gradually drifted together and fused to form a supercontinent called Pangea. This joining of continents reshaped the Earth's surface, creating a singular landmass surrounded by a vast ocean. The formation of Pangea was a pivotal event in Earth's history and had profound effects on the planet's climate, geology, and the evolution of life.
explanation_b: for some reason, pangea is embedded in the public consciousness, but pangea is just the most recent supercontinent and occurred relatively late in earth's history (occurring ~300 million years ago, compared to the ~4600 million year history of the earth). it's a relatively well established idea that the earth's plate go through what's called the [supercontinent, or wilson, cycle](_url_6_), namely that the formation of supercontinents happens with some frequency. as you can see from the wikipedia page, there have been a fair number of these proposed (pannotia, rodinia, columbia, kenorland, ur, vaalbara), but the evidence for them gets more problematic the farther you go back and there have been some questions about just how long the supercontinent cycle has been functioning. reconstructions of plate positions are based on various things, [paleomagnetism](_url_3_) being a major component. for the supercontinents formed during the history of life (so basically rodinia (sort of), pannotia, and pangea for critters that leave much of anything in the fossil record), distributions of fossils have played a role in reconstructing positions and orientations. locations of large mountain belts, formed during the collisional process and supercontinent assembly, like the [grenville orogeny](_url_7_) during the assembly of [rodinia](_url_2_), can also help us to reconstruct past locations. here is a link to a [series of paleogeographic maps](_url_0_) that present what the earth may have looked like based on datasets like the ones i described above, along with records of sedimentary rocks that tell us what types of environments were in different places at different times. you can see [pangea](_url_5_) during the early permian and [pannotia](_url_4_) during the late precambrian, and many times in between. beyond that, the record gets less and less complete so making these whole global reconstructions gets more challenging and the results are increasingly interpretive. you can check out the [parent page](_url_1_) for these reconstructions to look at these in other projections as well.

question: why can't we just look up at the moon with a telescope to where the astronauts landed to disprove conspiracy theorists?
explanation_a: The reasoning behind not being able to see the Apollo landing sites on the moon with a telescope from Earth is rooted in the enormous distance between the moon and our planet. The Apollo missions landed on the moon in the late 1960s and early 1970s, leaving behind equipment and structures that are incredibly tiny compared to the vast expanse of the moon's surface. To visualize this, imagine trying to spot a small coin on the ground from a flying airplane - the distance and the size of the object make it virtually impossible to see with the naked eye, let alone through a telescope. Furthermore, the resolution capability of even the most powerful telescopes on Earth is limited by factors such as atmospheric distortion and the diffraction of light. These factors, combined with the extreme distance to the moon, make it physically impossible to discern the Apollo landing sites through telescopes from Earth. To give an analogy, it's akin to trying to see a tiny ant crawling on a mountain peak from hundreds of miles away. Thus, while the technology and tools available have made great strides in exploring space, the moon's vast distance and the minuscule size of the landing sites render them invisible from our vantage point on Earth.

question: can a 4-d object spin in two directions?
explanation_a: To understand whether a 4-dimensional object can spin in two directions, we need to first establish some foundational concepts. In our everyday world, we often perceive objects as having three dimensions: length, width, and height. These dimensions allow us to describe the position and movement of objects in space. When an object like a ball spins in our three-dimensional world, it typically rotates around an axis, which could be vertical, horizontal, or diagonal. Now, let's think about a hypothetical 4-dimensional object. Just as a 2-dimensional object, like a flat sheet of paper, can spin in one direction (clockwise or counterclockwise), a 4-dimensional object, if it existed, could potentially spin along two distinct axes in two different directions simultaneously. This concept can be quite challenging to imagine since our everyday experience is limited to three dimensions. However, in the realm of theoretical mathematics and physics, the idea of multi-dimensional objects with unique rotational properties is a fascinating area of exploration.
explanation_b: mathematically, yes. 4 dimensions is the first vector space in which two independent rotations can occur without them summing to a single rotation in a single plane. for instance, an object can spin in the xy plane and also in the zw plane, simultaneously, and there is no single-"axis" spin which reproduces that motion (i say "axis" because rotations happen in 2d planes, and the rotation is only "around an axis" in 3d. in 4d the "axis" is another 2d plane.) i'm not sure how this applies to black holes though.

question: do the ants i'm flicking off of my backyard table feel pain?
explanation_a: no, they do not feel pain. whilst invertebrates do possess nociceptive ability (the detection of noxious stimuli), they do not experience pain as we, mammals, do. pain is a multifactorial experience in response to potential or actual tissue damage which has a sensory and affective components. this relies on the integration and summation of multiple different neuronal pathways. simply put, insects do not possess the neuronal capability to experience pain which includes key aspects of the pain aspect - notably the feeling of discomfort and displeasure. whilst they may withdraw from noxious stimuli (such as heat), this does not equate to the experience of pain.
explanation_b: Ants do not have the neurological complexity to feel pain in the way that animals with more advanced nervous systems like humans, mammals, or even some insects might experience it. Ants have very basic nervous systems, which lack the specialized structures required to process and interpret pain signals. When you flick ants off your backyard table, they may respond to stimuli like touch or temperature changes but not in the way we perceive pain. Think of an ant's brain like a very simple machine that can detect and respond to basic stimuli, but without the capacity to register pain. So, the ant may feel the force of being flicked off the table, but it isn't experiencing pain in the way we understand it. Whether the ant gets disturbed or not is more related to the sudden change in its environment rather than the sensation of pain.

question: what part of honey is antimicrobial?
explanation_a: The antimicrobial properties of honey are attributed to several key components found in it. One important component is hydrogen peroxide, which is produced by the enzymatic activity of glucose oxidase in honey. This compound has strong antimicrobial effects, capable of combating various pathogens like bacteria, fungi, and viruses. Furthermore, honey also contains other compounds like phenolic acids and flavonoids, which possess additional antimicrobial properties. These compounds work in synergy with hydrogen peroxide to create a hostile environment for microorganisms, helping to prevent infection and spoilage. Therefore, the antimicrobial nature of honey arises from a combination of factors, making it a natural and effective alternative to traditional antimicrobial agents.
explanation_b: oddly enough, it's the sugar. honey is so concentrated that it exerts tremendous osmotic pressure, essentially meaning that it sucks the water right out of micro-organisms. in addition, it's fairly acidic, and contains some hydrogen peroxide. you do have to keep honey sealed, or it will absorb moisture and eventually spoil.

question: why is string theory a "theory"? in science, doesn't "theory" mean something tested with reproducible results?
explanation_a: i can see how the usage of the word "theory" is confusing, especially since the colloquial and scientific usages of the word are already often confused. there is even a [similarly worded question](_url_2_) answered earlier today, but which actually asks a different question. that question asks about the scientific definition of "theory", its relation to the colloquial definition and whether scientific laws get somehow upgraded to scientific theories (or vice versa). the current question is actually asking about a third definition of "theory", which comes from mathematics. for something like string theory (which has no experimental evidence\*), the word "theory" is really meant in the *mathematical* sense and not the scientific sense. in mathematical logic, given some language and a set of a statements in that language (called axioms), we can talk about the *theory* of those axioms, which is the set of all statements that can be logically deduced from the axioms. so string theory is really a mathematical framework. for instance, [group theory](_url_0_) is the theory of the [group axioms](_url_1_). if instead we want to model physics, we may start with some mathematical structure that is required to make sense of the assumption that particles are not point-like but rather one-dimensional. in that case, the resulting set of statements is called a *string theory*. the usage of the word "theory" in *string theory* is very similar to its usage in *classical field theory* (cft) and *quantum field theory* (qft). cft and qft are simply mathematical frameworks that are useful for describing physics. classical electrodynamics and general relativity are both examples of a cft. quantum electrodynamics and quantum chromodynamics are both examples of a qft. the term "quantum field theory" is often understood to be synonymous with the standard model (which includes qed and qcd), but this association is not strictly true. sm is an example of a qft, whereas qft is a much more general term. the same goes for "string theory". --- \* string theory is consistent with current observations, and so technically has plenty of experimental evidence. so what i really mean is that there is no experimental evidence that distinguishes string theory, i.e., evidence that uniquely confirms string theory as a more accurate model than other current models. --- **edit:** just to clarify... a *quantum field theory* is a mathematical object, and the word "theory" is meant in the mathematical sense that i describe above. the *theory of quantum electrodynamics* is a scientific theory (and, therefore, well tested and corroborated), which is modeled mathematically as a *quantum field theory*. note the usage of the same word "theory" in two different senses in the terms *quantum field theory* and *theory of quantum electrodynamics*. for those with a bit more knowledge on the subject, consider that we can very well talk about the quantum field theory of φ^(3) in six dimensions despite it having no correspondence to the physical world. so the term *quantum field theory* covers a much wider range of objects than is implied by the common association of "qft" to "standard model". --- **edit 2:** i want to make clear that the term *string theory* is meant in the mathematical sense, and there are several string theories out there. there is not just one string theory, just as there is not just one quantum field theory. whether any particular string theory is an accurate description of our universe is somewhat irrelevant to calling it a theory. yes, any string theory (and, by that token, any quantum field theory) attempts to describe the universe, but that doesn't mean we cannot treat such formulations as pure mathematics. (in fact, there are unsolved mathematical problems in qft, even seemingly very basic ones. for instance, you can win a $1,000,000 prize for [proving that nonabelian gauge theory even exists and has a unique ground state](_url_3_), and the precise statement that you have to prove is a mathematical one, having nothing to do with physics per se.) --- **edit 3:** not directly related to the op's question... there are also several comments/lamentations/complaints that scientists are somehow aloof and have chosen terminology that only serves both to confuse the general public and to give opponents fodder for their denial (e.g., "it's just a theory!" in response to evolution, gmos, vaccines, climate change, or any other commonly denied scientific theory). on one hand, i share the disappointment that there are terms here and there that may have a scientific meaning that is different from the colloquial meaning and which may even have different meanings in different scientific fields. the term "theory" and related terms (like law, hypothesis, etc.) is not the only such term, although it is arguably the most notorious. i envy the scientist who has never felt frustration and/or disappointment in the face of scientific illiteracy, either at the individual or municipal level. on the other hand, it is important to understand that there is no committee of scientists that get together to define general science terms. (there may be specialized committees that define terms within a specific field, but that's different.) scientists and mathematicians do not get together to decide which terminology is best, and they certainly do not decide such terminology based on whether the general public will find it confusing. terminology just sort of gets passed around and then eventually sticks. it may even change later on. the crucial property of good terminology is really that experts understand it, not necessarily the general public. scientific illiteracy is a complex phenomenon and is not due solely or even primarily to possibly confusing terminology. laymen may become scientifically illiterate because of poor education (which occurs for a whole host of reasons). but scientific illiteracy in adulthood is certainly persisted by willful ignorance, poor scientific journalism, media sensationalism, and pseudoscience con artists who are more than willing to maintain and exploit such illiteracy. if we had a different term for "theory", we may not hear ridiculous protests like "it's just a theory!", but we would still witness plenty of other popular pseudoscience and denial tactics and arguments.
explanation_b: In the realm of science, the term "theory" has a specific meaning that might differ from its colloquial usage. A scientific theory, like string theory, is a well-developed explanation that has withstood extensive testing, scrutiny, and prediction of various phenomena. While a theory does indeed involve testing and reproducible results, it is important to understand that not all aspects of a theory might be directly testable. String theory, for instance, seeks to explain the fundamental particles and forces in the universe by proposing that these entities are made up of tiny vibrating strings. Although this concept is challenging to test directly with current technology, the theory provides a coherent framework that unifies quantum mechanics and general relativity. Even though not all components of a theory may be immediately testable, the broader framework can make testable predictions that align with existing experimental data. Scientists continue to explore ways to test various implications of string theory, such as through high-energy particle collisions or astronomical observations. So, while string theory may not fit perfectly into the traditional notion of a theory that can be easily tested in a laboratory, its ability to provide a comprehensive and elegant explanation for the fundamental workings of the universe earns it the title of a scientific theory.

question: does day-old coffee lose its caffeine content?
explanation_a: unlike all of the other posters in this thread, i have done this experiment. a cup of brewed coffee left st room temperature for 24 hours had about 60% of its caffeine remaining. there's been lots of talk of caffeine's chemical stability, but it's a carbon and nitrogen source for bacteria. edit: also, coffee left at 4 degrees celsius for 2 weeks had less than 5% of its original caffeine content. the method of assaying caffeine was capillary electrophoresis, a pretty reliable method. edit 2: all right, i'm being misinterpreted so even though i'm on my phone i'll hunt and peck keys and take the time to explain how all this came about. this is absolutely an anecdote, i did not repeat the experiment, the results are not published, and i don't even have a lab notebook to show you because i was working as a technician for a college and was demonstrating the ce machine. the students had their lab books, but this was 3 years ago and we haven't kept in touch. i brewed a cup of coffee in the employee lounge, then diluted it and ran caffeine standards and integrated the peak areas of standards and sample. so fine, we found out how much coffee was in that particular cup. each pair of students replicated the experiment, and iirc there was a decent standard deviation. i'm afraid i don't remember the caffeine concentration, but it was close to the "litetaturev value" i got from some nutrition website. there were too many students to all do the experiment the same day, so half the class was supposed to repeat it the next day. i showed up in the lab and realized i'd forgotten to brew fresh coffee. but luckily, yesterday's coffee was still next to the machine, uncovered, in some coffee mug i'd found in the lounge. we did the experiment, again 4 times, and found the caffeine content was about 40% lower. i took this as an opportunity to troubleshooting with the students... the standards peak areas were the same as yesterday's so the machine was functioning properly. the best we could come up with is microbiological action. we did not in any way attempt to prove this was the cause, it was an analytical chem class, not microbiology. the next week we ran the experiment again with a fresh cup and got reasonably close to the first group's results. then i put the rest of that coffee in a bottle in the fridge in case someone wanted to use the ce again. someone did, and found very little caffeine. i hope i've explained the context adequately, and i apologize for phone-caused typos. i don't think i wad making overreaching claims, and i apologize if i wasn't't clear what i was claiming. normally i wouldn't have posted such informal results in askscience, but the thread was full of assurances caffeine concentration would not decrease and nobody had considered microbiological factors so i felt like adding this perspective.
explanation_b: When it comes to caffeine content in day-old coffee, let's simplify the concept by understanding how caffeine behaves. Caffeine is a stable compound, which means it doesn't break down easily. Therefore, the caffeine content in coffee typically remains relatively stable over time. However, other compounds in coffee can change as it sits, affecting its taste and overall quality. These changes may make the caffeine feel less potent due to altered flavors and aroma rather than an actual decrease in caffeine content. To illustrate this, think of caffeine as a sturdy rock in a stream that remains unchanged over time, while the water around it may shift and change. So, while day-old coffee may not have less caffeine, its taste and overall experience can be compromised due to other factors such as oxidation and flavor degradation. So, your morning pick-me-up might not taste as fresh, but the caffeine kick remains largely intact.

question: why is the higgs boson listed separately from the other gauge bosons in the standard model?
explanation_a: because the higgs boson is not a gauge boson. gauge bosons are spin 1 particles that are needed to ensure that a local symmetry holds. the higgs boson is a spin 0 particle and it does not serve to ensure the existence of a local symmetry.
explanation_b: In the Standard Model of particle physics, the Higgs boson is distinct from the other gauge bosons for a specific reason. While gauge bosons like photons, W and Z bosons, and gluons are responsible for mediating the fundamental forces of nature (electromagnetic, weak nuclear, and strong nuclear forces), the Higgs boson plays a unique role in giving mass to other particles through the Higgs mechanism. This process is what we call the Higgs field, which permeates space and interacts with particles, imparting mass to them. Without this interaction with the Higgs field, particles would not have mass, and the universe as we know it would be very different. Imagine the Higgs boson as the "celebrity" of the Standard Model, standing out from the other particles by its unique function of giving mass to other particles. Just like how a famous celebrity may have a distinct role in a movie, the Higgs boson has a distinct role in the universe's fundamental forces. Hence, it holds a special place in the Standard Model alongside the other gauge bosons, highlighting its crucial role in shaping the mass of particles and, ultimately, the structure of the universe.

question: are commercial airplanes flying as fast as they can fly?
explanation_a: they're not flying as fast as is *possible*, but they are flying the speed that makes economic sense. fortunately for impatient travelers everywhere. those speeds are very nearly equivalent. take the boeing 787 as a typical airliner. its top speed is mach 0.9, and its cruise speed is mach 0.85 (at 35,000 feet). the difference between those speeds is only about 5%. the reason cruise speed is lower than maximum speed is that cruise speed is where the plane is most fuel-efficient, and therefore a) has the highest range and b) can carry the most passengers. the pilots *might* "step on the gas a bit" if they can get away with it (passengers and range vs remaining fuel allow them to increase thrust) but that costs the airline more money, so i suspect if they want to do such a thing they need to get special permission from the dispatcher.
explanation_b: Commercial airplanes do not typically fly at their maximum speed for a few reasons. Firstly, airlines prioritize fuel efficiency over speed to keep operating costs down. Flying at lower speeds saves fuel, making it more cost-effective for airlines. Secondly, flying at lower speeds can also reduce wear and tear on the aircraft, extending its lifespan and reducing maintenance costs. While commercial airplanes have the capability to fly faster than their typical cruising speeds, they are designed to operate within a certain range for optimal performance. Pilots adhere to specific speed limits and flight plans to ensure the safety and comfort of passengers. It's similar to driving a car - you could go faster, but it may not be the best choice for fuel efficiency, safety, and vehicle longevity.

question: if we can't hear transmissions from somewhere like kepler 452b, then what is the point of seti?
explanation_a: Imagine SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) as a giant cosmic radio station trying to tune in to different frequencies to pick up signals. Just like how you might turn the dial on a radio trying to catch a particular station, SETI is focused on scanning the vast universe for signs of intelligent life by listening for any potential transmissions coming from distant planets like Kepler-452b. Now, even if we might not currently be able to pick up any broadcasts or signals from such faraway places, SETI's ongoing efforts serve a critical purpose. The ultimate goal is that someday, just like turning that radio dial and suddenly catching a clear signal, SETI could intercept a communication from an alien civilization. This possibility fuels the curiosity and imagination of scientists and space enthusiasts alike, driving the search for potential cosmic neighbors and expanding our understanding of the universe. In essence, SETI represents a pioneering quest to listen to the cosmic symphony, hoping to catch a unique tune that could revolutionize our understanding of life beyond Earth. While we may not have heard any transmissions from Kepler-452b yet, the excitement lies in the anticipation of that one day when we might just intercept a signal that could change everything we know about our place in the vast cosmos.
explanation_b: seti claims to be able to detect roughly earth-like signals up to a distance of about 1000ly ([here](_url_0_)). of course the actual distance depends on the power of the transmitted signal, and for sure when it arrives at earth it will be very weak compared to other naturally occurring radio sources in the universe, which is one of the reasons the seti project is hard. there are 511 stars within 100ly, ~280,000 within 500ly, and the nearby stars are the low hanging fruit. it would be idiotic of us to not check them for the obvious signs of intelligent life first, even if it turns up nothing.

question: why do we still use rockets to get into space?
explanation_a: One of the fundamental reasons why rockets are still used to access space is due to Newton's third law of motion, which states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Rockets work by expelling gases at high speeds in one direction, which propels the rocket in the opposite direction with an equal force. This principle allows rockets to generate thrust in the vacuum of space where there is no air for traditional engines to push against. Despite advancements in technology, rockets remain the most practical way to overcome the Earth's gravity and reach orbital speeds necessary to enter space. Other potential alternatives like space elevators or electromagnetic launch systems are still in the realm of theoretical research and face significant engineering challenges. Furthermore, rockets are versatile and have been continuously improved over the years in terms of efficiency, payload capacity, and reliability, making them the preferred choice for space exploration and satellite deployment missions.
explanation_b: "up" is not the issue. "fast" is the issue. a typical airplane cruises at or below about five hundred miles an hour. in order to get into low-earth orbit, you have to accelerate to *seventeen thousand* miles an hour. that takes propellant. a lot of it. a space shuttle on the launching pad weighs four and a half million pounds. that's the same as six fully-loaded 747s.

question: how did the double slit experiment explain if light was a wave or a particle?
explanation_a: interference patterns only happen with waves. detection of objects at point locations only happens with particles. in the double slit experiment, light (or electrons, or whatever), are shone through two slits to create two coherent beams that can potentially experience interfere. the result of the experiment is that on the photographic plate you indeed get an interference pattern, but the pattern is composed of a smattering of point-wise detections. therefore, the light is both a wave and a particle. if it were just a particle, you would not get the interference pattern. if if were just a wave, you would not get the point-wise detections. look at [this image of the double slit experiment perfomed with electrons](_url_0_). you see both dots and bars, meaning that electrons are both particles and waves. you get the same kind of result with light (but you need much more sensitive equipment to actually run the experiment with light). update: as others have mentioned, the more accurate statement is: light is neither a classical wave nor a classical particle, but is something more complicated which acts in certain ways like a wave and in other ways like a particle, at the same time. if this sounds vague to you, its not because quantum theory is vague. the theory itself is concrete, predictive, quantitative, self-consistent, and complete in its own realm. the hard part is turning the equations of quantum theory into little qualitative pictures that humans can visualize in their minds based on things they are used to in everyday life. that is where the vagueness of quantum theory arises, and that is where the wording gets clumsy. calling a quantum object a classical wave or a classical particle, or both is not strictly accurate, but is a useful mental shortcut for humans to use in making a picture in their mind.
explanation_b: Imagine a stage with two small slits, like two doors, through which tiny particles can pass. In the double-slit experiment, when light, which we thought of as waves, was shone through these slits, an intriguing pattern emerged on the screen behind them. Instead of just two bands of light that you might expect from particles passing through two slits, there were multiple bands of light and dark areas, known as interference patterns. This behavior was more consistent with waves interacting with each other rather than individual particles passing through. This observation led scientists to believe that light may behave more like a wave than a particle. However, the plot thickened when the experiment was conducted with very low light intensity, revealing something remarkable - the appearance of individual light particles, or photons, hitting the screen one at a time. Over time, these individual impacts still formed an interference pattern! This fascinating discovery suggested that light had characteristics of both waves and particles, leading to the groundbreaking concept of wave-particle duality – the idea that light can exhibit properties of both waves and particles depending on the context.

question: why do we need to compile separate 32 and 64 bit versions?
explanation_a: Imagine your computer is like a bilingual person who can understand both English and Spanish. When a program is written, it's like having a conversation—a set of instructions—from the developer to the computer. Now, think of 32-bit and 64-bit as different languages. question: are radio waves affected by the dopler effect, why don't i hear a distortion as i'm driving towards or away from a radio station?
explanation_a: Yes, radio waves are indeed affected by the Doppler effect, a phenomenon where the frequency of waves changes based on the relative motion between the source of the waves and the observer. In the case of a moving vehicle, as you drive towards a radio station, the frequency of the radio waves increases, and as you drive away, the frequency decreases. The reason you don't typically notice distortion when driving towards or away from a radio station is because the frequencies involved are relatively low, and the human ear is not as sensitive to minor changes in frequency as it is to changes in amplitude (loudness). In contrast, if you were dealing with higher frequencies like visible light, where the Doppler effect is more noticeable, you would see a shift in color as you move towards or away from a source. So, even though the Doppler effect is at play with radio waves while you're driving, the changes in frequency are not significant enough for your ear to perceive as distortion.
explanation_b: the doppler shift is small because the radio waves travel at the speed of light ("c"), not the speed of sound, and a car is quite slow compared to c. example: a 30 m/s car speed is 10% of the speed of sound but only 10^-7 times the speed of light, or 0.1 part per million. what effect does that have? consider a 100 mhz fm radio station. the frequency would shift up by 10 hz as you are driving towards the station, to 100.000 010 mhz. that's a much smaller change in frequency than the ~75 khz range of variation in frequency than is being used to encode the audio (by fm = frequency modulation). so the radio receiver won't notice the difference. then there's the effect that the audio signal encoded by that modulation will be sped up by a factor of 1.0000001. a musical half step is about a 6% change. the smallest increment in tuning that musicians (or organ turning technicians talk about is a "cent", equal to 1/100th of a half step. in some situations, some highly trained people can hear a fraction of a cent difference. this is 1/6000th of a cent.

question: is there a certain amount of "real estate" at the a given lagrangian point? could we potentially put too many stations, observatories, or other spacecraft there and run out of room?
explanation_a: Lagrange points are specific positions in space where the gravitational forces of a two-body system, like the Earth and the Moon, produce enhanced regions of attraction and repulsion. There are five Lagrange points in such a system, denoted as L1 to L5. These points have a somewhat limited "real estate" in the sense that they represent positions where the gravitational forces are balanced. While these points offer stable orbits for spacecraft due to the delicate balance of forces, they are limited in size and are essentially points in space. Therefore, in theory, these points could become overcrowded if too many stations, observatories, or spacecraft were to be placed there. However, due to the vastness of space compared to the relatively small size of objects placed at Lagrange points, it would take a significant number of spacecraft to truly overcrowd these points. It's more likely that spacecraft would spread out to maintain safe distances from each other and prevent collisions rather than actually running out of physical space at these points.
explanation_b: sort of. the further you are from the lagrangian point, the further your actual behavior will be from the theoretical behavior exactly at the lagrangian. at an unstable lagrangian, that means that the further you are from it, the faster you will diverge from the point. a station that wanted to sit at an unstable lagrangian would need to periodically make small adjustments to its trajectory to "realign". the further from the actual precise point you are, the more frequent and larger those adjustments would need to be. at a stable lagrangian, that means the further you are from the point, the less of a stabilizing effect you will experience; your orbits around the stable point will be larger and less predictable. a station at a stable lagrangian could do without course-corrections, depending on how much "meandering" you're willing to accept. as you get far enough away, you would realistically need course-corrections in order to avoid other objects (like the other stations). both effects are gradual; there wouldn't be a sharp cutoff between "this station is in the 'lagrangian zone' and this other one is not." edit: obviously, the assumption is that you have to have some space between the actual objects you're putting up. if you are imagining these stations/spacecraft being literally pressed up against each other, there's effectively limitless (by earth standards) real estate. but in practice you will want quite a bit of separation.

question: what is the purpose of a prostate, and why does it cause problems for older men?
